en: The Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga:
The Section on Offenses Entailing Expiation (Pācittiyakaṇḍa)
Sappāṇakavagga 65.
The Training Rule on Those Under Twenty Years of Age.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Place.
Now at that time, there were seventeen young boys in Rājagaha who were companions;
the boy Upāli was their leader.
Then it occurred to Upāli’s mother and father:
“By what means, Upāli, might you live happily after our passing and not come to exhaustion?
Then it occurred to Upāli’s parents:
“If Upāli were to train in writing, then he would live happily after our passing and not come to exhaustion.”
Then it occurred to Upāli’s mother and father:
“If Upāli trains in writing, his fingers will suffer pain.
But if Upāli were to train in calculation, then after our passing, he would live happily and not be exhausted.”
Then it occurred to Upāli’s parents:
“If Upāli trains in calculation, his chest will suffer pain.
But if Upāli were to train in painting, then after we have passed away, he would live happily and not be exhausted.”
Then it occurred to Upāli’s parents:
"If Upāli trains in the art of painting, his eyes will suffer.
These ascetics, the sons of the Sakyans, are easy in their habits and easy in their conduct; having eaten fine foods, they sleep on beds sheltered from the wind."
“If, Upāli, you were to go forth among the recluses who are followers of the Sakyan son, then, Upāli, after we have passed away, you would live happily and not suffer.
The boy Upāli overheard this conversation between his mother and father.
Then the boy Upāli went to where those other boys were; having approached them, he said this to those boys:
“Come, noble ones, let us go forth among the ascetics, the sons of the Sakyan.
“If you, noble one, will go forth, then we too shall go forth.
Then those children approached each of their parents and said this:
“Grant me permission to go forth from the home life into homelessness.
Then those children’s parents, thinking,
“All these children have the same desire and the same noble intention,” gave their consent.
Having approached those monks, they requested the going-forth.
Those monks granted them the going-forth and conferred full ordination upon them.
Then, rising at the time of dawn during the night, they wept.
“Give us rice gruel! Give us cooked rice! Give us solid food!
The bhikkhus said, “Wait, friends, until the night has turned to dawn.”
If there is rice gruel, you shall drink it;
if there is cooked food, you shall eat it;
if there is fresh food, you shall eat it.
“If there will be no rice gruel, nor cooked rice, nor hard food, you shall eat after wandering for alms.
Even though they were addressed thus by the monks, those monks continued to weep, saying, “Give us rice gruel!
Give us cooked rice! Give us hard food!”
They were even snoring and snorting in their lodgings.
The Blessed One, having risen at the time of dawn during the night, heard the sound of the children.
Having heard it, he addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
“What, Ānanda, is that sound of children?
Then the Venerable Ānanda informed the Blessed One of the matter.
Thereupon, on this occasion and in this connection, the Blessed One had the community of monks assembled and questioned the monks:
“Is it true, monks, that you knowingly ordain a person who is less than twenty years of age?
“It is true, Blessed One.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them … [as before] …
“How, monks, can those foolish men knowingly ordain a person who is less than twenty years of age?
A person less than twenty years of age, monks, is unable to endure cold, heat, hunger, thirst, the touch of gadflies,
mosquitoes, wind, sun, and creeping things, as well as abusive and offensive speech that has arisen.”
He is by nature unable to endure bodily feelings that are painful, sharp, harsh, bitter, disagreeable, unpleasant, and life-threatening.
Monks, a person who is only twenty years old is capable of enduring cold, heat... [and so forth].
He is by nature one who endures things that take away life.
This, monks, does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence...
And furthermore, monks, you should recite this training rule as follows:

“Whatever bhikkhu, knowing that a person is less than twenty years of age, should confer full ordination upon him, that person is not fully ordained and those bhikkhus are blameworthy; this is a *pācittiya* offense for him.
“Whatever bhikkhu” means whichever one... [and so forth].
"Bhikkhu" ...
[as before] ... this is the "bhikkhu" intended in this context.
"Knows" means:
He knows it himself, or others inform him of it, or he informs [others] himself.
"Less than twenty years old" means one who has not reached twenty years of age.
If, thinking, “I shall confer full ordination,” he searches for a group, a preceptor, an alms bowl, or a robe, or he demarcates a boundary, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
For the motion (ñatti), there is an offense of wrong-doing.
For two proclamations (kammavācā), there are offenses of wrong-doing.
At the conclusion of the formal act (*kammavācā*), the preceptor commits an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*);
the community and the teacher commit an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
If one ordains someone who is less than twenty years of age while perceiving them to be less than twenty, it is an offense of expiation.
If one ordains someone who is less than twenty years of age while being in doubt, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If one ordains someone who is less than twenty years of age while perceiving them to be twenty years of age, there is no offense.
If one ordains someone who is twenty years of age while perceiving them to be less than twenty years of age, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If one is doubtful whether [the person] has completed twenty years, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If [the person] has completed twenty years and one perceives them as having completed twenty years, there is no offense.
There is no offense—
If one ordains someone who is less than twenty years old while perceiving them as being full twenty years old;
or if one ordains someone who is full twenty years old while perceiving them as being full twenty years old;
or in the case of one who is insane.
"For one who is a first offender":
thus ends the fifth training rule concerning those under twenty years of age.
